title: Automatically Retrofitting JIT Compilers
gist: Laurence Tratt demonstrates yk, an open-source meta-tracing JIT framework that retrofits a just-in-time compiler onto existing C interpreters with ~400 added lines (under 5% of the Lua codebase), yielding roughly 2x geomean on Lua benchmarks and 4x on a cherry-picked Mandelbrot. The core bet is that the existing C interpreter — not a rewrite in a host language, as RPython and Truffle require — must be treated as the source of truth, which is what lets the JIT track upstream language releases instead of stagnating like LuaJIT and the graveyard of abandoned Python JITs.

themes.theme: Measured performance and cost of retrofit

insights.claim: A standard Lua VM running a Mandelbrot benchmark took 3.2 seconds versus 0.8 seconds under the yk-forked Lua, roughly 4x, though the speaker openly identifies this as a cherry-picked best case.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Establishes an upper bound for retrofit JIT gains on dynamic languages and, unusually, the presenter discloses the selection bias — treat the geomean, not the demo, as the planning number.
insights.quote: Now, you can bet your bottom dollar I have cherry-picked this example of something rotten.
insights.locator: Now what I'm going to do is our fork of this same Lua VM

insights.claim: Across a wider set of Lua benchmarks the yk retrofit delivers a geometric mean of roughly 2x, with the speaker projecting 3x as plausible once escape analysis and further optimizations land.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: A 2x-to-3x free speedup on unmodified scripting workloads is the realistic value proposition to weigh against rewriting hot code in a faster language.
insights.locator: Across a wider set of Lua benchmarks

insights.claim: MicroPython on the Fannkuch benchmark ran 15 seconds unmodified and about 2x faster under ykmicropython, achieved with under 10 person-days of engineering investment.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: The marginal cost of adding a new language target collapses from person-years to person-days, which is the whole economic argument for meta-tracing.
insights.locator: If we have a look at MicroPython on the well-known Fannkuch benchmark

insights.claim: Retrofitting yk onto the Lua VM required adding about 400 lines and changing about 50, under 5% of the codebase.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: The small, non-invasive diff is the mechanism that makes tracking upstream language releases tractable — the failure mode that killed prior JITs.
insights.quote: We've added 400 lines. We probably could have got away with adding fewer, and changed about 50.
insights.locator: Those changes you saw to yklua

insights.claim: Because the change surface is only 400 lines concentrated in stable parts of the interpreter, keeping the JIT current with a new upstream language release is roughly an afternoon of rebasing.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Directly attacks the structural reason alternative VMs die — maintenance drift — and is the claim to stress-test if evaluating yk for production use.
insights.quote: There's 400 lines of code. I reckon I can rebase that in an afternoon.
insights.locator: Participant 2: Then does that mean that if they release a new version of Lua

insights.claim: The instrumentation tax is severe: with the JIT switched off, a yk-compiled interpreter runs roughly 3x to 4x slower than normal because of the shadow stack, recording functions, and disabled LLVM optimizations.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: The reported speedups are net of a large handicap, meaning the JIT itself is doing far more than 2x of work — but also that short-running or non-loopy programs will regress badly.
insights.quote: Roughly, and this is going to vary, the interpreter without the JIT on is going to be 3x, 4x slower than normal.
insights.locator: There are, though, consequences

insights.claim: Nearly all publicly available just-in-time compilers built for Python are dead or effectively abandoned, despite a long list of independent attempts.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: A graveyard this large is the base rate any new language-runtime project should be underwritten against.
insights.quote: Nearly all of these are dead or abandoned in such a way that they might as well be dead.
insights.locator: These are the publicly available just-in-time compilers I know of for Python

insights.claim: Production-grade JIT compiling VMs demand extraordinary capital: HotSpot has absorbed low thousands of person-years and V8 is maintained by a team of 50.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Quantifies the moat around incumbent runtimes and explains why only companies with browser or platform economics can sustain one.
insights.locator: Say that the main Java virtual machine HotSpot has had low thousands of persons of years

insights.claim: JIT compilers fail commercially through three compounding mechanisms — subtle incompatibility with the mainstream implementation, incompatibility with the module and extension ecosystem, and inability to evolve when the language spec changes — with LuaJIT cited as stuck on an old Lua version.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on alternative runtimes is compatibility maintenance, not peak performance — a diagnostic for evaluating any 'faster drop-in' claim.
insights.locator: There are other issues. If you make a new implementation

insights.claim: Users abandon an alternative language implementation permanently after a single failed run, giving new runtimes essentially one attempt at adoption.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Explains why drop-in compatibility, not benchmarks, is the go-to-market gate for runtime products.
insights.quote: People try your thing out. It doesn't quite run your program straight away. You ditch it, move on. You never try it again.
insights.locator: If you make a new implementation, I say maybe

insights.claim: The intrinsic difficulty of JIT VMs is that a minimal error produces catastrophic, hard-to-localize failure, making the engineering both slow and expensive.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Debuggability, not algorithmic novelty, is the cost driver in runtime engineering — relevant to estimating timelines for any compiler project.
insights.quote: You make the smallest slip, things go splat, and you will be debugging it for a week.
insights.locator: I would say fundamentally, it's because just-in-time compiling VMs are really hard

insights.claim: Performance is typically ignored until it becomes an emergency, with organizations moving from indifference to existential panic within a day.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Explains the bursty, urgency-priced demand pattern for performance tooling — buyers appear suddenly and without budget planning.
insights.quote: My experience is that often people go from not caring about performance to thinking it's an existential crisis in under 24 hours.
insights.locator: Why? Why are we doing this?

insights.claim: The cheapest performance intervention — swapping in a faster language implementation such as PyPy for CPython for a 3x-5x gain — is routinely overlooked in favor of profiling, algorithmic rewrites, or porting to a faster language.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: A near-zero-effort lever most engineering orgs skip; worth checking before funding a rewrite.
insights.locator: They often miss one of my favorite techniques

themes.theme: The source-of-truth bet that differentiates yk

insights.claim: The de facto standard C interpreters — CPython, MRI/CRuby, the Lua VM — are the real source of truth for their languages, because published specifications are incomplete and users validate programs by whether they behave correctly on the standard implementation.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: The insight that reframes the whole problem: any runtime not derived from the reference implementation inherits an unbounded compatibility liability.
insights.quote: Those standard implementations which are nearly always C interpreters are the source of truth.
insights.locator: Most of this awkward squad of languages we're talking about have de facto standard implementations

insights.claim: Once the C interpreter is accepted as the source of truth, generating a meta-tracing JIT from that C interpreter is the only viable technique — partial evaluation and other approaches do not follow from that premise.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Frames yk's architecture as forced by its premise rather than chosen, which is the strongest form of a technical differentiation argument.
insights.quote: I don't think other techniques work, or at least I don't know how to make them work.
insights.locator: We realized we had to take this as our source of truth

insights.claim: The two prior automated-JIT technologies, RPython (meta-tracing, same project family as PyPy) and Truffle (partial evaluation), both require rewriting the interpreter in a host language — a Python subset or Java respectively — and consequently drift onto older language versions and stay incompatible.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Locates yk's competitive wedge precisely: same automation goal, but no interpreter rewrite, hence no version drift.
insights.locator: There are two basic approaches which happily exemplified

insights.claim: HotSpot, despite being arguably the best JIT compiler ever built and now containing three JIT compilers, is a poor vehicle for some languages — Jython, Python on the JVM, is genuinely slow — which is what leaves room for language-specific automated JIT projects.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Undermines the assumption that a world-class general runtime subsumes specialized ones; guest-host semantic mismatch is not solvable by compiler quality alone.
insights.quote: HotSpot is not a great vehicle for running some kinds of languages, which is why there's room for a project like this.
insights.locator: Participant 1: I'm sort of a Java developer background

insights.claim: Method-based JIT compilers like the JVM's find hot functions and compile them, whereas tracing JITs find hot loops and record the actions taken during one concrete iteration, then optimize and compile that linear trace.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: The core taxonomy for reasoning about runtime performance work; concrete-execution recording is why tracing inlines aggressively for free.
insights.locator: If you're making a JIT compiling VM, the typical way it's done

insights.claim: Meta-tracing records what the C interpreter does while executing a hot loop in the guest program, rather than recording the guest program's own opcodes — the inversion that lets one tracing engine serve any interpreter.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: The single conceptual move that converts per-language compiler work into a reusable framework — the reason marginal language cost drops to person-days.
insights.locator: Meta-tracing, and this is the weird bit

insights.claim: yk works by compiling the interpreter through ykllvm, a fork of LLVM that inserts path-recording functions into the binary and serializes a simplified form of LLVM IR into the executable, so traced path IDs can later be stitched back into optimizable IR at runtime.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: The build-time mechanism is a compiler-flag-level drop-in, which is what keeps integration cost near zero for interpreter authors.
insights.locator: How do we actually get from a C program to this running system

insights.claim: Conditional branches in a trace become guards, and the compiled trace remains valid only while every guard holds; a false guard forces deoptimization back to the interpreter.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Guards are the unit of speculative risk in a tracing JIT — fewer guards means faster code but costlier reconstruction when speculation fails.
insights.locator: The way to think of this

insights.claim: JIT-compiled code takes over the C interpreter's stack rather than allocating its own frame, so deoptimization requires LLVM stack maps at safepoints — placed wherever control flow can diverge — to restore every live variable to the exact register or stack offset Clang's ahead-of-time build expects.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Explains why deoptimization is the hardest part of retrofit JITs and why it depends on niche compiler infrastructure.
insights.locator: Somehow, when we hit a guard that's false

insights.claim: Because C code can take the address of a stack variable that becomes invalid after deoptimization, yk maintains a second shadow stack per thread holding stable addresses, making the transition between JIT and interpreter modes completely transparent to the interpreter.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: A concrete engineering pattern for retrofitting speculative execution onto pointer-taking C code — and a named source of the baseline slowdown.
insights.locator: For better or for worse, we have to have a second shadow stack

insights.claim: LLVM stack maps are an under-polished feature: some optimization passes do not respect them and some code generators emit instructions in invalid places, forcing yk to disable optimizations for reliability.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: A named upstream infrastructure gap; improving LLVM stack map support would directly unlock performance for this whole class of tooling.
insights.quote: Stack maps, they're not exactly an afterthought in LLVM, but they are a less loved feature.
insights.locator: There are, though, consequences

themes.theme: Developer hints as the performance lever

insights.claim: Interpreter-author hints, not generic compiler optimizations, dominate yk's performance: removing a single four-line yk_idempotent annotation asserting that a Lua function's opcodes never change slowed the Mandelbrot benchmark from 0.8 to 2.93 seconds, a 3.5x regression.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: The value of an automated JIT is unlocked by a handful of semantic annotations — a live demonstration that domain knowledge beats general optimization by multiples.
insights.quote: It's not quite as slow as the normal Lua implementation, but we've slowed it down 3.5x, just by removing that hint.
insights.locator: This little four-line function that I've inexpertly highlighted

insights.claim: A single yk_promote call added to Lua's arithmetic macro promotes a runtime value of 8 to 64 bytes to a trace-level constant with a guard behind it, which is what turns a Lua source integer into an x86 immediate and collapses a load-add-store sequence into one instruction.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Shows the mechanism concretely: constant promotion plus guard is the primitive that converts dynamic-language flexibility into static machine code.
insights.locator: All we did was we added a simple call to a function called yk_promote

insights.claim: Optimizing away guards is itself a major source of speedup: the 3.5x-slower configuration likely carried around five times as many guards as the fast version, since constantness proofs eliminate guards entirely.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Guard count is the observable proxy for how much semantic information the interpreter author has exposed — a tuning metric for anyone adopting yk.
insights.locator: What I haven't fully been able to show you is, when we compile a trace

insights.claim: Guard overhead never reaches zero even with good branch prediction, and traditional interpreters are surprisingly branch-predictor-unfriendly unless they use threaded dispatch, which resolves the next opcode target at the end of each opcode rather than returning to a central switch.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: A reusable low-level fact for interpreter performance work independent of any JIT decision.
insights.locator: Participant 3: I'm also new to JIT

insights.claim: Pushing speculation to the limit of one guard per program is not workable, because tracing records a concrete execution without lookahead and cannot know in advance which future state will violate the trace.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Bounds how far the constant-promotion technique can be pushed — guard density is structurally required, not just conservative engineering.
insights.locator: Participant 3: You could almost push that to the limit of no guards

insights.claim: Whether a source-level loop is actually a traceable loop is indeterminate at trace time: if the loop's entry condition happens to fail on the traced iteration, the recorder jumps past the body, never closes the loop, and can wander into extremely long useless traces.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: The structural failure mode of tracing, and the reason performance can be erratic rather than merely mediocre.
insights.locator: Here's a Lua loop. Let me ask you a question. Is this a loop?

insights.claim: The bad-trace problem can be ameliorated with heuristics that abandon recording when a trace fails to close, but it can never be fully eliminated because recording begins without knowing what will execute.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: An honest permanent limitation to weigh when choosing tracing over method-based compilation for a given workload profile.
insights.quote: You can't ever fully fix it because you start recording not knowing what you're about to execute.
insights.locator: Fundamentally, there is no way around this

insights.claim: The industry overgeneralized from TraceMonkey, Firefox's first JavaScript VM, concluding that all tracing compilers are bad when the real lesson was that one particular VM was weak.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: A case study in how one high-profile failure can freeze a technical approach for a decade — worth checking wherever an approach is 'known' to be dead.
insights.quote: People have then, to my mind, overgeneralized from that that all tracing compilers are bad.
insights.locator: I want to give you a sense of a different challenge

insights.claim: yk is open source, alpha quality and explicitly not production ready, though the author positions it well beyond a typical research prototype.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Sets the adoption timeline honestly — this is a technology to track, not deploy, in the current cycle.
insights.quote: I'm presenting alpha quality software here. It's not production ready, but it is way beyond your average research prototype.
insights.locator: Recap

insights.claim: The work is funded by Shopify and the Royal Academy of Engineering, with Tratt holding the Shopify / Royal Academy of Engineering Research Chair in Language Engineering at King's College London.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Shopify's sponsorship of Ruby-adjacent runtime research is a signal about where large Ruby-dependent operators expect performance gains to come from.
insights.locator: We're very lucky this work was being funded by Shopify

insights.claim: yk currently runs only on x86 and lacks support for parts of LLVM including vector instructions and vector types, though the machine-specific work is fully transparent to interpreter authors so an ARM backend would require no interpreter changes.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Architecture portability is an engineering-only cost for this design, which matters given the ARM server share; vector-type gaps limit numeric workloads today.
insights.locator: What's Next?

insights.claim: The roadmap targets escape analysis — eliding heap allocations that never escape a loop iteration — as the next major speedup, followed by Pico Python and eventually CPython and CRuby, which are described as no harder intellectually but far larger in feature surface.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: The milestone that would make this commercially consequential is CPython or CRuby support; everything before that is a proof of scaling.
insights.locator: We would like to do more optimization

insights.claim: Interpreter authors adopting yk must expose loop locations and constantness to the framework, so integration is not free of semantic work even though it is free of platform-specific work.
insights.speaker: Laurence Tratt
insights.so_what: Scopes the real adoption cost for a language maintainer: semantic annotation effort, not compiler backend expertise.
insights.quote: You will have to adjust your interpreter a bit for yk, because you want to expose this constantness thing, and you have to tell it where loops are a bit.
insights.locator: Participant 1: Do you have to do machine instruction setups
